newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin's daughter gets Kremlin post.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin's daughter gets Kremlin post.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, who celebrates the first anniversary of his re-election this week, finally gave official credit to the daughter who helped keep him in the Kremlin by naming her his official image-maker on Monday.
"By decree of the president...Tatyana Borisovna Dyachenko is named adviser to the president," Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky intoned drily during a routine news briefing.
Asked what precisely the 37-year-old Tatyana would advise her father on, he replied simply: "The president's image."

The announcement was long expected. The blonde mathematician and mother-of-two has been a fixture in the Kremlin since the early days of last year's campaign, providing her father with a "reality check" among his cliques of professional advisers.

"There are unpleasant things which it's easy only for me to tell him," Dyachenko told NTV television in an interview on Monday, citing as an example the slump in Yeltsin's popularity this year. "I can do it with tact and choose a convenient moment. I know him very well and I know how to tell him this."

"He'll get the view of a common sense person," she said, echoing remarks about her by the man closely identified with her induction into the inner circle of power, former campaign boss and now the government's liberal economy chief, Anatoly Chubais.
She also told NTV she helped prepare Yeltsin's weekly radio talks which she hoped brought the president closer to the people and revealed the real man and the reasons for his decisions.

During the election campaign, Dyachenko was credited with helping Chubais persuade Yeltsin to ditch hawks like bodyguard Alexander Korzhakov, who is her younger son Gleb's godfather. Korzhakov has turned bitterly against Yeltsin and his family.

Dyachenko helped soften a presidential image coarsened by the war in Chechnya. She told NTV she had insisted Yeltsin shake off his stony-faced entourage during campaign walkabouts so that he was seen on television surrounded by smiling ordinary people.
The change of image was a stunning success bringing Yeltsin back from deep unpopularity to beat his communist rival on July 3.

When the strain felled him days before his re-election and he then spent months convalescing from multiple heart bypass surgery in November, Kremlin aides said Tatyana and Chubais became the ubiquitous gatekeepers for the 66-year-old president.

Some Kremlin insiders complained Dyachenko had too much sway over her father. And her closeness to Chubais -- so close the first deputy premier had to deny they were lovers -- earned her the hostility of the communist and nationalist opposition.
Dyachenko, though quick to welcome her father's move to end confusion about her role, said she was bracing for criticism.
"The president decided that this way there would be less ambiguity," she told NTV.
"I'm morally prepared for people writing unkind -- and untrue -- things about my work," she told Interfax news agency.

Kremlin sources said one reason the announcement was made now was that the opposition-dominated State Duma lower house of parliament began its summer recess last week. Yeltsin faced charges of nepotism recently after the husband of his elder daughter Yelena was named head of the state airline, Aeroflot.
Dyachenko has taken tips from Claude Chirac, daughter of the French president, who advises her father.

Married to Alexei Dyachenko, she was born in the Urals city of Sverdlovsk, now Yekaterinburg, where Yeltsin was to become Communist party chief. While at university in Moscow in 1981 she gave birth to a son by her first husband. Now at school in England, the teenager has his grandfather's name, Boris Yeltsin.
Dyachenko told NTV she and her husband live with her father, mostly at an official residence outside Moscow. Her mother Naina and a nanny look after their infant son Gleb, born in 1995.
